idiom_name: one struct per node type implementing a Node interface + type switch
implementation_notes: Go has no sum types and no inheritance, so node kinds are separate structs whose fields are the named children, tied together by a small interface - the standard library's go/ast is the reference design (BinaryExpr{X Expr; OpPos token.Pos; Op token.Token; Y Expr} implementing Node through Pos() and End()). Traversal is written per node type with a type switch or a hand-written Walk-style function, and the C-style tag-and-cast is unnecessary because the interface value already carries the concrete type. Keep this form while the tree is small or the passes are few, and add a normalized children accessor if generic tooling appears.
pitfalls: A type switch has no exhaustiveness check: adding a node type leaves every existing walker silently incomplete, so walkers need an explicit default that panics or reports.
An interface holding a typed nil pointer is not nil, so child checks must test the concrete pointer value, not the interface.
Structs are copied on assignment: pass nodes as pointers so identity and any in-place mutation stay coherent.
